saint_pick.name: Vitalis and Agricola
saint_pick.selection_reason: The master Vitalis and his slave Agricola, martyred together at Bologna around 304, make a moving, surprising story: the slave goes to the cross first while the master encourages him, and Ambrose, who found their relics in 393, left a firsthand account. It is better documented than Emeric's legendary Life, and the story is about equality in Christ.
saint_pick.catholic_veneration: Listed in the Roman Martyrology on 4 November as martyrs of Bologna; their relics are venerated in the Basilica of Santi Vitale e Agricola in Bologna.

beats.text: Agricola watched his own slave die for Christ, then chose the same.
beats.scene: An icon of a bearded Roman citizen in a plain tunic and cloak standing at the edge of an arena, gazing with calm resolve at a young man in a slave's simple tunic who holds a martyr's palm. Tiers of stone seats rise behind them under a gold sky.

beats.text: Saints Agricola and Vitalis, of Bologna in Italy, about the year three hundred and four.
Agricola was a Christian, beloved for his gentleness. He led his slave, Vitalis, to the faith. The two grew deeply attached.
beats.scene: An icon of a gentle older Roman man in a tunic and mantle resting a hand on the shoulder of a younger man in a plain servant's tunic. They stand together in the courtyard of a fourth-century Roman house with columns and a small fountain.

beats.text: In the persecution under Diocletian, Vitalis was the first to die, in the amphitheatre. Almost everything we know comes from Saint Ambrose.
beats.scene: An icon of the young Vitalis in a plain tunic, standing with arms open and eyes lifted to heaven in the middle of a Roman amphitheatre. Stone arches and a crowd of small figures appear behind him, and a martyr's palm rests at his feet.

beats.text: Tradition holds that the persecutors hoped this would break Agricola. Instead it gave him courage. He was crucified.
beats.scene: An icon of Agricola in a plain tunic, his face serene, standing before a wooden cross in the amphitheatre. A halo shines around his head, and Roman soldiers in the background look on.

beats.text: In three ninety-three, Ambrose and Bishop Eusebius moved their remains from a Jewish cemetery into a church. Ambrose then carried relics to Milan and Florence.
beats.scene: An icon of Saint Ambrose in bishop's vestments and Bishop Eusebius, with clergy and townspeople, carrying a reliquary in procession into a late-Roman basilica with round arches and mosaics. Candles and incense fill the doorway.

beats.text: The Church honors them together, a master and his slave, as brothers in Christ. Faith made them equal.
beats.scene: An icon of Agricola in a mantle and Vitalis in a plain tunic standing side by side, each holding a martyr's palm. Their halos are of equal size, and a gold background with a simple basilica sits behind them.

beats.text: Saints Vitalis and Agricola, pray for us.

claims.claim: Vitalis and Agricola are venerated as martyrs who died at Bologna about 304 during Diocletian's persecution.
Agricola was a Christian citizen of Bologna, beloved for his gentleness.
Agricola converted his slave Vitalis to Christianity, and the two became deeply attached to each other.
Vitalis was the first to suffer martyrdom, executed in the amphitheatre.
Ambrose's mention of the martyrs in his oration is the only authority for their lives.
The persecutors hoped Vitalis's sufferings would make Agricola abandon his faith, but it strengthened him instead.
Agricola was crucified.
Both martyrs were buried in the Jewish graveyard.
In 393 Ambrose and Bishop Eusebius of Bologna transferred the remains of the martyrs to a church.
Ambrose transferred some relics to Milan and gave some to Florence.
The Roman Martyrology lists them on 4 November as martyrs of Bologna.
In 396 other relics were sent to Victricus, Bishop of Rouen, and to Paulinus of Nola.
Ambrose placed relics at Florence in a church built by the widow Juliana and gave an oration in praise of virginity, with special reference to her three virgin daughters.
A basilica was built at Bologna to hold the relics.
The church of San Vitale ed Agricola in Arena is purported to stand over the remains of a Roman amphitheatre; its crypt of the two martyrs dates to the eleventh century.
Gregory of Tours at the end of the sixth century lamented that no passio of the two martyrs existed.
Paulinus of Nola attests their fellowship in martyrdom, and Ambrose and Paulinus give the oldest record of them.
Their cult was already widespread in the fifth and sixth centuries, and Bologna remained its center.
Their witness as slave and master is taken as a message of equality and solidarity, recognized publicly in the free commune's decree liberating serfs.
The Roman Martyrology says Vitalis suffered such torments that no part of his body was without wound, and that Agricola, unafraid, imitated him in martyrdom by crucifixion.
Feast day is 4 November.
Vitalis and Agricola are patrons of Salsomaggiore Terme.

story: Bologna in the early fourth century was a Roman city in northern Italy. Around the year 304, the emperor Diocletian's persecution reached it. Out of that time come two names, Agricola and Vitalis, a Christian citizen and his slave. The Church has long honored them together as the first martyrs of Bologna.

We know very little about their lives, and it is best to say so plainly. Nearly everything rests on what Saint Ambrose, the bishop of Milan, said of them in an oration he gave at the end of the fourth century. The Catholic Encyclopedia calls that mention the only authority for their lives. What follows is the account the Church has handed down, which is why we tell it as tradition.

Agricola was a citizen of Bologna and a Christian, and he was beloved for his gentleness. He had a slave named Vitalis. According to the tradition, Agricola led Vitalis to Christ, and the two became deeply attached to each other. In the Roman world, a master and a slave stood at opposite ends of society. In the faith they shared, they were brothers.

When the persecution came, the tradition holds that both were brought to the amphitheatre. Vitalis was the first to die there. The Roman Martyrology says he endured terrible sufferings. Then the persecutors turned to Agricola. According to the account, they hoped that seeing Vitalis suffer would break his resolve. It had the opposite effect. Agricola was strengthened by the death of his slave and friend, and he faced crucifixion with courage, keeping his witness to the end.

For a time, it seems, the two were nearly forgotten. They had been buried in the city's Jewish cemetery, and Santi e Beati notes they were unknown until the early 390s, when Bishop Eusebius of Bologna announced the discovery of their remains. In 393 Ambrose came to Bologna, and he and Eusebius transferred the remains to a church with Christian rites. The Catholic Encyclopedia names that year as the date of the transfer. The people of the city began to venerate the martyrs from that time.

Ambrose then did much to spread their memory. He took some relics to Milan and gave others to Florence. There he placed relics in a church built by a devout widow named Juliana, and he gave an oration in praise of virginity that mentioned Agricola and Vitalis and honored her three daughters. In 396, further relics were sent to Victricus, the bishop of Rouen, and about the same time to Paulinus of Nola. Paulinus also wrote of them and spoke of their fellowship in martyrdom.

Even so, at the end of the sixth century Gregory of Tours lamented that no account of their passion existed. Their cult nonetheless endured, with Bologna as its center. A basilica was built to hold their relics, and the church of San Vitale ed Agricola in Arena is purported to stand over the Roman amphitheatre where they died. Its crypt of the two martyrs dates to the eleventh century. Today the Roman Martyrology lists them on 4 November as martyrs of Bologna, and they are patrons of Salsomaggiore Terme.

Later Bolognese tradition saw in the pair a message of equality and solidarity. It is said to have been publicly recognized when the free commune decreed the liberation of serfs. Santi e Beati preserves a prayer of the Church of Bologna that speaks of the fraternal solidarity of slave and master, a bright example of humanity reconciled in the love of Christ. Little else survives of Vitalis and Agricola, but that is enough to remember them by.

issues: Spoken beat 'Everything we know comes from Saint Ambrose' is too absolute. Source 2 says Paulinus of Nola also attests them, although Source 1 calls Ambrose the only authority for their lives. Changed to 'Almost everything'.
Spoken beat said Ambrose carried relics to 'Florence and Milan' after the 393 transfer. Source 0 gives the order as Milan, then Florence. Reordered.
The script came to about 124 spoken words, just under the 125 minimum. The 'Almost' addition and 'as brothers in Christ' bring it to about 126.
Caption and YouTube title said they were 'martyred together'. The sources say Vitalis died first and Agricola later, as 'companions in martyrdom'. Reworded to 'martyrs of Bologna'.
Story paragraph 1: 'the Church there was small and often hidden' is not in the sources. Removed.
Story paragraph 2: 'Everything rests on' conflicts with Source 2, which names Paulinus as well. Changed to 'Nearly everything'.
Story paragraph 5: 'For decades' is unsupported. The sources say only that they were unknown until 392. Changed to 'For a time'.

Map (Bologna, 44.4949, 11.3426) is correct. Titles are correct: 'Saints' for early martyrs, 'Bishop' for Eusebius, feast on 4 November. Hook is under 14 words and the legend beats are marked as tradition.

The hook's 'watched' rests on Santi e Beati saying both were led into the arena. Sources also differ on the bishop's name (Eusebius vs Eustasio) and the year (392 vs 393); the script follows the Catholic Encyclopedia.

issues: Hook was 14 words; the rule is under 14. Trimmed to 13 and kept the 'Tradition says' framing.

Story beat 3 (spoken), claim 5 and story paragraph 4 say Agricola himself was tortured. That follows Wikipedia, but the Catholic Encyclopedia, the Roman Martyrology and Santi e Beati say Vitalis was the one tortured. Agricola faced flattery and the sight of his servant's sufferings, then crucifixion. Fixed the beat, the claim and the paragraph to follow the Catholic references.
Story paragraph 2: 'Most accounts say' implies several independent accounts, but the sources only give the one tradition. Changed to 'The tradition says'.
Story paragraph 2: 'Nothing is recorded of their families or their daily lives' and 'a household' are not in the sources. Softened to 'Little is known of their daily lives' and removed 'household'.

Story paragraph 4: 'Since then the Church has called them the first martyrs' implies this title dates from their deaths, but the cult began only in 392 or 393. Changed to 'Today the Church calls them'.

es.name: San Vital y San Agrícola
es.hook: Un amo y su esclavo, hermanos en Cristo, mártires de Bolonia.
es.summary: Agrícola de Bolonia llevó a Cristo a su esclavo Vital, y cuando Vital murió primero en la persecución de Diocleciano, Agrícola lo siguió hasta la cruz.
story: Bolonia a comienzos del siglo IV era una ciudad romana en el norte de Italia. Hacia el año 304, la persecución del emperador Diocleciano llegó hasta ella. De aquella época proceden dos nombres, Agrícola y Vital, un ciudadano cristiano y su esclavo. La Iglesia los ha honrado desde hace mucho tiempo juntos como los primeros mártires de Bolonia.

Sabemos muy poco sobre sus vidas, y conviene decirlo con claridad. Casi todo se apoya en lo que san Ambrosio, obispo de Milán, dijo de ellos en un discurso pronunciado a finales del siglo IV. La Enciclopedia Católica llama a esa mención la única autoridad sobre sus vidas. Lo que sigue es el relato que la Iglesia ha transmitido, por eso lo contamos como tradición.

Agrícola era ciudadano de Bolonia y cristiano, y era querido por su mansedumbre. Tenía un esclavo llamado Vital. Según la tradición, Agrícola llevó a Vital a Cristo, y los dos llegaron a estar profundamente unidos. En el mundo romano, el amo y el esclavo ocupaban extremos opuestos de la sociedad. En la fe que compartían, eran hermanos.

Cuando llegó la persecución, según la tradición, ambos fueron llevados al anfiteatro. Vital fue el primero en morir allí. El Martirologio Romano dice que soportó terribles sufrimientos. Entonces los perseguidores se volvieron hacia Agrícola. Según el relato, esperaban que ver sufrir a Vital quebrantara su firmeza. Tuvo el efecto contrario. Agrícola se fortaleció con la muerte de su esclavo y amigo, y afrontó la crucifixión con valentía, manteniendo su testimonio hasta el final.

Durante un tiempo, al parecer, los dos fueron casi olvidados. Habían sido enterrados en el cementerio judío de la ciudad, y Santi e Beati señala que permanecieron desconocidos hasta comienzos de los años 390, cuando el obispo Eusebio de Bolonia anunció el descubrimiento de sus restos. En 393 Ambrosio llegó a Bolonia, y él y Eusebio trasladaron los restos a una iglesia con ritos cristianos. La Enciclopedia Católica señala ese año como la fecha del traslado. Desde entonces, el pueblo de la ciudad comenzó a venerar a los mártires.

Ambrosio hizo luego mucho por extender su memoria. Llevó algunas reliquias a Milán y entregó otras a Florencia. Allí colocó reliquias en una iglesia construida por una viuda devota llamada Juliana, y pronunció un discurso en alabanza de la virginidad en el que mencionó a Agrícola y Vital y honró a sus tres hijas. En 396 se enviaron más reliquias a Victricio, obispo de Ruán, y por la misma época a Paulino de Nola. Paulino también escribió sobre ellos y habló de su comunión en el martirio.

Aun así, a finales del siglo VI Gregorio de Tours lamentaba que no existiera ningún relato de su pasión. Su culto, sin embargo, perduró, con Bolonia como centro. Se construyó una basílica para albergar sus reliquias, y según se dice la iglesia de San Vital y San Agrícola en Arena se levanta sobre el anfiteatro romano donde murieron. Su cripta de los dos mártires data del siglo XI. Hoy el Martirologio Romano los recuerda el 4 de noviembre como mártires de Bolonia, y son patronos de Salsomaggiore Terme.

La tradición boloñesa posterior vio en la pareja un mensaje de igualdad y solidaridad. Se dice que esto fue reconocido públicamente cuando la comuna libre decretó la liberación de los siervos. Santi e Beati conserva una oración de la Iglesia de Bolonia que habla de la solidaridad fraterna entre esclavo y amo, un luminoso ejemplo de la humanidad reconciliada en el amor de Cristo. Poco más sobrevive de Vital y Agrícola, pero basta para recordarlos.
es.prayer: San Vital y San Agrícola, rueguen por nosotros.
